title: Feelings with Layers
objectives: I can use ten words to describe mixed and complex feelings.
I can tell the difference between dread, dismay, regret, and resentment.
I can find clues in a story that show how a character feels and why.
I can write about a time I felt two things at once, using words from this unit.
rationale: The last unit of grade 5 turns students inward. By now they can describe a character as happy or sad, but literature at grade 6 asks them to name feelings with layers: the sweet and the sad together (bittersweet), the heavy fear before something happens (dread), the wish for something far away (longing, yearn), the shame of a past choice (regret), and the anger that builds when treatment feels unfair (resentment). Dismay, contentment, anticipation, and composure fill in the rest of the range, from shock to quiet peace to control. Eight of the ten words are nouns that name a feeling, so students learn that the same noun pattern (contentment, resentment, anticipation, composure) comes from familiar verbs and adjectives. The passage follows a girl on the day her family moves, so that mixed feelings are shown in one clear situation. Reminisce, ominous, dignity, and nostalgia return from earlier units because memory, mood, and self-respect all shape how a person feels about change.

words.def: Both happy and sad at the same time.
words.ex: Graduation day was bittersweet for the class, who were proud but sad to say goodbye.
words.ex2: The old song brought a bittersweet smile to her face.
words.nonExample: A day of pure joy with no sadness is not bittersweet.

morph.note: Bittersweet is a compound of bitter and sweet.

apps.academic: Authors use a bittersweet ending to show that gains and losses can come together.
apps.writing: Use bittersweet for a feeling or event that is both happy and sad.

cloze.s: The last day of summer camp felt ___, since we had loved the weeks but did not want to leave our friends.

cloze2.s: It was a ___ moment when the old teacher retired, because we were glad for her rest but sad to see her go.

misuse.s: The bittersweet party was only happy, with no sadness at all.
misuse.why: Bittersweet means happy and sad together; a party that is only happy is not bittersweet.

words.frame: Saying goodbye to ___ felt bittersweet because ___.

words.def: Strong fear about something that may happen.
words.ex: Jen felt dread each time she thought about the big test.
words.ex2: A sense of dread filled the room when the lights went out in the storm.
words.nonExample: Looking forward to a party is not dread.

apps.academic: Writers use dread to build suspense in a story.
apps.spoken: I have a dread of the dentist.
apps.writing: Use dread for fear of something that has not happened yet.

cloze.s: As the dentist's door opened, a feeling of ___ made Marcus grip the arms of the chair.

cloze2.s: The campers felt ___ as the thunder grew louder and the tent shook in the wind.

misuse.s: She felt dread about her birthday party because she could hardly wait for the fun to begin.
misuse.why: Dread is fear of something that may happen; looking forward to fun is not dread.

visual.alt: A worried face next to an hourglass.

words.def: A deep wish for something or someone you do not have.
words.ex: The immigrant felt a longing for the village where she grew up.
words.ex2: With a look of longing, the boy watched the other children play on the playground he could not reach.
words.nonExample: Having everything you want is not longing.

apps.academic: Poets often write about longing for home or for the past.
apps.spoken: He gazed out the window with longing.
apps.writing: Use longing for a deep wish, often mixed with sadness.

cloze.s: As the ship sailed away from her island, she felt a deep ___ for the voices of her family.

cloze2.s: The puppy watched the mailman with ___, wishing he could run outside and play.

misuse.s: The boy felt a deep longing for the toys he already owned and played with every day.
misuse.why: Longing is a deep wish for something you do not have; he already has the toys.

visual.alt: A far-off house under a sunrise.

words.frame: I feel a longing for ___ when ___.

words.def: A sad feeling about something you did or did not do.
words.ex: Leo felt regret for forgetting his friend's birthday.
words.ex2: She has no regret about the long walk, though her feet hurt.
words.nonExample: Being proud of a kind choice is not regret.

apps.academic: A writer may show a character's regret through an apology.
apps.spoken: I have no regrets about the trip.
apps.writing: Use regret for sadness about a choice made in the past.

cloze.s: After snapping at her little brother, Mara felt a deep ___ and hurried to say she was sorry.

cloze2.s: He felt ___ at having left the project until the last minute, since the grade was low.

misuse.s: Her regret was a feeling of pride about the perfect choice she had made.
misuse.why: Regret is sadness about a past choice; pride in a perfect choice is not regret.

visual.alt: A sad face with a rewind symbol.

words.def: A sudden feeling of shock and worry at bad news.
words.ex: The crowd groaned in dismay when the game was canceled.
words.ex2: To her dismay, the cake had fallen flat just before the party.
words.nonExample: A quiet smile at good news is not dismay.

apps.academic: A writer may show dismay with a gasp or a fallen face.
apps.spoken: Much to my dismay, I lost my notes.
apps.writing: Use dismay for a sudden feeling of worry and disappointment about news.

cloze.s: The team looked at the scoreboard with ___ when they saw they were behind by twenty points.

cloze2.s: To Ava's ___, the rain began just as she finished setting out the picnic.

misuse.s: He jumped with dismay at the news that he had won the grand prize.
misuse.why: Dismay is shock and worry at bad news; winning a prize is not dismay.

visual.alt: A worried face under a rain cloud.

words.def: A quiet feeling of being satisfied and happy with what you have.
words.ex: The cat purred in contentment as she curled up by the fire.
words.ex2: After a long hike, Jamal sat on the porch with a sense of contentment.
words.nonExample: A feeling of wanting something more is not contentment.

apps.academic: Many writers describe contentment as a calm and lasting form of happiness.
apps.spoken: I felt contentment on the beach.
apps.writing: Use contentment for a quiet, settled happiness.

cloze.s: With a warm blanket, a good book, and rain tapping the roof, Olivia felt perfect ___.

cloze2.s: The farmer looked over his full barn and sighed with ___ at a good harvest.

misuse.s: The child was full of contentment, so he paced and complained and asked for something new every minute.
misuse.why: Contentment is quiet satisfaction; pacing and asking for something new shows restlessness.

visual.alt: A relaxed face next to a steaming cup.

words.def: Bitter anger about being treated unfairly.
words.ex: Resentment grew in him each time his brother got special treatment.
words.ex2: She spoke with resentment about the rule that only some students could use the playground.
words.nonExample: A calm thank-you for fair treatment is not resentment.

apps.academic: Historians describe how resentment over unfair taxes led some people to protest.
apps.spoken: I felt a bit of resentment when she got extra time.
apps.writing: Use resentment for a long-lasting bitter feeling about unfair treatment.

cloze.s: After being left out of the game again, Jose felt ___ toward the captain who picked only his friends.

cloze2.s: The workers' ___ over the unfair pay grew until they asked for a meeting with the manager.

misuse.s: She felt resentment because everyone had been fair and kind to her.
misuse.why: Resentment is anger about unfair treatment; fair, kind treatment does not cause it.

visual.alt: An angry face next to scales that are uneven.

words.def: A feeling of excited waiting for something you expect to happen.
words.ex: The children waited at the window in anticipation of the first snow.
words.ex2: The audience filled with anticipation as the lights dimmed before the show.
words.nonExample: Forgetting that an event is coming is not anticipation.

segs.m: to expect or look forward to

apps.academic: Anticipation can make a short wait feel very long.
apps.spoken: I'm full of anticipation for the field trip.
apps.writing: Use anticipation for the feeling of waiting for something you expect.

cloze.s: The class buzzed with ___ as the teacher unwrapped the box that held the new class pet.

cloze2.s: Her eyes glowed with ___ on the night before the big trip.

misuse.s: They waited in anticipation for a day that had already passed and was long forgotten.
misuse.why: Anticipation is excited waiting for something that has not happened yet.

visual.alt: A wrapped gift beside an hourglass.

words.def: To want something very much, especially something far away or lost.
words.ex: The sailor would yearn for home during the long months at sea.
words.ex2: After a week of rain, the campers began to yearn for sunshine.
words.nonExample: Casually liking a snack is not to yearn for it.

apps.academic: Poets often use yearn to show a deep wish for a person or a place.
apps.writing: Use yearn for a deep and lasting wish, stronger than want.

cloze.s: During the cold, dark winter, the villagers began to ___ for the warm days of spring.

cloze2.s: Far from his family, the young soldier would ___ for the sound of his mother's voice.

misuse.s: He did not care about the gift, but still yearned for it with all his heart.
misuse.why: To yearn is to want deeply; not caring about the gift contradicts that.

visual.alt: A distant sunrise with a thought bubble.

words.def: Calmness; control of your feelings in a hard moment.
words.ex: The pilot kept her composure when the plane began to shake.
words.ex2: Though he felt nervous, Sam spoke with composure to the whole school.
words.nonExample: Screaming in panic is not a sign of composure.

apps.academic: Debaters need composure so that they can answer hard questions clearly.
apps.spoken: She kept her composure during the race.
apps.writing: Use composure for calm control of feelings when something is hard.

cloze.s: When the lights went out in the middle of her speech, the principal kept her ___ and waited calmly.

cloze2.s: The goalie kept his ___ even after the crowd began to boo him.

misuse.s: She showed great composure by screaming and throwing her papers when the alarm rang.
misuse.why: Composure is calm control; screaming and throwing papers show panic, not composure.

passage.title: The Last Day on Maple Street
paras: On the last morning before the moving truck came, Lina walked through her empty room. She felt bittersweet: excited about the new city, yet sad to leave the only home she remembered. A week earlier she had felt only dread, a heavy fear in her stomach whenever she pictured the new school.

At the kitchen table, her father unfolded a map of the new neighborhood. Lina felt a flutter of anticipation about the green park near the school. Only days before, she had felt resentment toward her parents for choosing the move, and she still had regret about the sharp words she had said to them. "I'm sorry," she told them quietly.

Omar waited on the porch with a small box. When the truck rumbled up the street, his face fell with dismay, but Lina kept her composure, though her throat felt tight. Inside the box was a smooth stone from the creek where they used to play. "So you will not forget us," he said. Lina felt a longing for those afternoons, and she yearned to freeze the day so that nothing would change.

But time kept moving, and as the truck pulled away, a quiet contentment settled over her. She had friends, a stone from the creek, and a map with a green park. Feelings, she thought, can be sad and hopeful at once.

qs.q: In paragraph 1, the word "bittersweet" most nearly means
choices: both happy and sad at the same time
qs.why: Lina is excited about the new city but sad to leave her home, so bittersweet means both happy and sad.

qs.q: What does the word "dread" tell the reader about how Lina felt about the new school?
choices: She was afraid of what it would be like.
She had already made friends there.
qs.why: The author describes dread as a heavy fear in her stomach whenever she pictured the new school.

qs.q: Which detail best shows that Lina felt regret?
choices: She walked through her empty room.
She kept her composure on the porch.
She had regret about her sharp words and told her parents she was sorry.
She took a stone from the creek.
qs.why: The text says she still had regret about sharp words and then apologized, which shows regret.

qs.q: Why did Lina keep her composure when the truck arrived?
choices: She wanted to stay calm even though she felt sad.
She did not care that the truck came.
She was too excited to speak.
qs.why: Her throat felt tight and she was sad, yet she stayed calm, so composure means control of feelings in a hard moment.

qs.q: Which sentence best states the main idea of the passage?
choices: Lina's feelings about leaving were mixed, with sadness and hope together.
Omar was angry at Lina for leaving.
A new park is better than an old creek.
qs.why: Lina feels bittersweet, dread, regret, longing, and contentment in one day, and she ends by saying feelings can be sad and hopeful at once.

teacher.overview: Students learn ten words for layered feelings: bittersweet, dread, longing, regret, dismay, contentment, resentment, anticipation, yearn, and composure. The passage follows a girl on her last day in her old home, so many feelings appear in one setting. Study of the -ment, -ure, and -ion endings shows how the verbs and adjectives students know become nouns that name feelings.

notes.va.bittersweet.adj: Bittersweet is a compound adjective for feelings that are happy and sad together. It can also describe a taste. Students may think a bittersweet feeling is half-and-half; teach that both are strong at once. Collect examples from stories.
notes.va.dread.n: Dread is fear about what may come. It is more about a coming event than a present danger. As a noun it means the feeling; as a verb, to fear something coming. Ask students to place dread on a worry ladder.
notes.va.longing.n: Longing is a strong wish for something or someone not here. It pairs with yearn, a verb. Students may think longing is only sadness; teach that it can mix sadness with hope. Link to nostalgia from unit 7, which is longing for the past.
notes.va.regret.n: Regret is a sad feeling about something done or not done. It is different from guilt or blame. Ask students to name a small regret and a larger one. Note that regret can also be a verb, as in I regret saying that.
notes.va.dismay.n: Dismay is a sudden feeling of worry or disappointment at something unexpected. It is stronger than annoyance and weaker than despair. Ask students to show a dismayed face and then describe it in words.
notes.va.contentment.n: Contentment is a quiet satisfaction with what one has. It is not excitement. Students often think contentment means laziness; teach that it is a settled peace. The base is content, and -ment makes a noun.
notes.va.resentment.n: Resentment is bitter anger over a feeling of unfair treatment. It tends to last. Link to injustice from unit 4: injustice can produce resentment. Note the spelling of resent plus -ment.
notes.va.anticipation.n: Anticipation is excited waiting, often for something good, though it can also mean expecting something bad. Contrast with dread, which expects something bad. Ask students to compare the feeling before a trip with the feeling before a test.
notes.va.yearn.v: Yearn is a verb for wanting something deeply, often something lost or far away. It is stronger than want or wish. Pair it with the noun yearning and with longing.
notes.va.composure.n: Composure is calm control of feelings in a hard moment. It is a noun. Students often think composure means not feeling anything; teach that the person feels strongly but stays in control. Use the porch scene as a model.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'The passage says Lina is excited about the new city but sad to leave her home. Two feelings at once means bittersweet. The text says she kept her composure even though her throat felt tight, so she was sad but stayed calm. I can check each feeling word against a detail in the story.'

teacher.reviewAdvice: Revisit reminisce, ominous, dignity, and nostalgia by asking students how nostalgia mixes with longing, how an ominous mood can lead to dread, and how composure relates to dignity. Return to the ten words after two days, again at one week, in a short character study.

needsReview: Spanish glosses not reviewed by a native speaker: agridulce (bittersweet), pavor (dread; temor also used), añoranza (longing), arrepentimiento (regret), consternación (dismay), satisfacción (contentment), expectativa (anticipation), anhelar (yearn), compostura (composure).
Morph notes for composure (compose + -ure, with compose meaning to calm or settle) and anticipation (anticipate + -ion) are standard but were not checked against an etymological dictionary.
Teacher note says anticipation can also mean expecting something bad; this is a standard but less common use and a human reviewer should confirm.
